text: Doctor Heidegger took from the black book a withered rose, whose green leaves and crimson petals had assumed one brownish hue, so that it seemed ready to crumble to dust. <break time="0.8s" /> This rose, said the doctor with a sigh, was given to me fifty five years ago by Sylvia Ward, whose portrait hangs yonder, and I meant to wear it at our wedding. <break time="0.8s" /> He then threw the faded flower into the water of the vase, and, to the astonishment of all, its crushed petals began to stir and to deepen in color. <break time="0.8s" /> Did you never hear of the Fountain of Youth, asked Doctor Heidegger, which Ponce de León, the Spanish adventurer, went in search of two or three centuries ago. <break time="0.8s" /> That fountain is situated in the southern part of Florida, and a friend of mine, knowing my curiosity in such matters, has sent me what you see in the vase. <break time="0.8s" /> The guests, though they did not believe a word of it, agreed to drink, for they thought that the experiment would be harmless at worst. <break time="0.8s" /> Before you drink, my respectable old friends, said the doctor, it would be well that you should draw up a few general rules for your guidance in passing a second time through the perils of youth. <break time="0.8s" /> Think what a sin and shame it would be if, with your peculiar advantages, you should not become patterns of virtue and wisdom to all the young people of the age. <break time="0.8s" /> The doctors four venerable friends made him no answer except a feeble and tremulous laugh, so ridiculous was the idea that they would ever go astray again.
